senses.gloss:
padārtha
(‘object,’ ‘category’)
------------------------------------------
This word is used in several senses such as the meaning of a word, an object and a category.
The last one is a technical term used in the वैशेषिक दर्शन and comprises seven padārthas.
See VAIŚEṢIKA-DARŚANA.

Padmapurāṇa
------------------------------------------
Education and culture should go together. Or, rather, that which imparts culture alone is true एदुचतिओन्. This is exactly what the पुराणस् did in the olden days when formal एदुचतिओन् given in the gurukulas was restricted to the three higher castes.
Out of the eighteen major purāṇas—called Mahāpurāṇas—the Padmapurāṇa (or Pādmapurāṇa) is the second.
There seem to be two recensions—the Bengal recension and the South Indian recension—of this purāṇa, though it is only the latter that has been printed.
The total number of granthas or verses is 55,000 distributed among 690 adhyāyas or chapters accommodated in six khaṇḍas or books.
This purāṇa has been classed among the sāttvika (and Vaiṣṇava) पुराणस्.
A very brief synopsis of its contents may now be attempted.
1. Ādikhaṇḍa (62 chapters)
This khaṇḍa is sometimes called Svargakhaṇḍa also. Geographical details of ancient India (called जम्बूद्वीप and भारतवर्ष), description of a large number of tīrthās (places of पिल्ग्रिमगे) including the rites and formalities connected with visiting them are described here. प्रयाग (modern Allahābād) containing the त्रिवेणी saṅgama (the confluence of the three rivers गङ्गा, यमुना and the subterranean सरस्वती) is eulogised as the best of all the tīrthas. Code of conduct and the duties of the four āśramas are also delineated.
2. Bhūmikhaṇḍa (125 chapters)
This book is perhaps named as Bhūmikhaṇḍa to show the importance of this bhūmi or earth where alone spiritual progress is possible.
Performance of one’s duty is stressed here as important like a tīrtha or a holy place, since it purifies one who does it. Incidentally a number of stories are narrated, bringing out the importance of devotion to one’s parents, repetition of Lord Hari’s name and certain aspects of धर्म. Description of स्वर्ग (heaven) and नरक (hell) are also given briefly.
3. Brahmakhaṇḍa (26 chapters)
This is the shortest of all the books.
The name of this book does not seem to have any direct connection with the contents.
Devotion to Lord विष्णु, importance of physical service in a temple, greatness of the Kṛṣṇajayantī festival, virtuous deeds to be performed by which one can get good children, significance of एकादशी vrata (vow), the power of Lord Hari’s name and what offends it—these are the topics dealt with here.
4. Pātālakhaṇḍa (113 chapters)
In this book there is a detailed description of the Aśvamedhayāga (Horse-sacrifice) performed by राम. Unlike Valmīki’s Rāmāyaṇa, here सीता is reunited with राम and lives for many more years.
The battles between लव and कुश on one side and the army of राम on the other, are described in great detail.
The latter part of this purāṇa is devoted to describing the story and the greatness of कृष्ण. The गोपीस् of वृन्दाबन् are stated here, to be the ṛṣis or the sages of the त्रेतायुग who had been captivated by the beauty and charm of राम, reborn to enjoy his company.
Incidentally, information about śālagrāmas, a special मन्त्र of कृष्ण and its repetition, पूजा of Lord विष्णु, characteristics and effects of true भक्ति or devotion, are also explained.
It is interesting to note that in this book, the greatness of शिव, his emblem (the लिङ्ग) and his name as also the importance of भस्म (holy ash) are also given a wide coverage.
5. Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa (82 chapters)
Though this book is called Sṛṣṭi-khaṇḍa, the topic of सृष्टि or च्रेअतिओन् is only a minor aspect of the subjects dealt with.
Apart from the stories connected with the देवस् (gods) and the दानवस् (demons), the topic of śrāddha (obsequial rites) is dealt with in detail. The other subjects delineated are: sacrifice performed by ब्रह्मा; the story of the sage अगस्त्य subjugating the विन्ध्य mountain; some vratas or religious observances; story of महिषासुर; the arising of a golden lotus from the navel of विष्णु; birth of ब्रह्मा from this lotus; characteristics of a bad and a good ब्राह्मण; greatness of a पतिव्रता (chaste woman); importance of various kinds of दान or gifts; on the rudrākṣī beads and the तुलसी leaves; significance of the worship of गणेश; and, finally on the worship of the नवग्रहस् (nine प्लनेत्स्) and the goddess दुर्गा.
6. Uttarakhaṇḍa (282 chapters)
The title ‘uttara’ for this book simply signifies ‘last’. It is the last of the series of khaṇḍas comprising this purāṇa.
The contents of this book may be briefly summarised as follows:
Greatness of certain places of pilgri-mage like Śrīśaila and हरिद्वार as also the rivers गङ्गा and यमुना; importance of annadāna or gifting ड़ोओद्; description of the 24 ekādaśis (eleventh days of every fortnight); Viṣṇusahasranāma (which is different from the one given in the Mahābhārata); description and greatness of the Vaiṣṇavas (devotees of विष्णु); battles between the gods and the demons; worship of शालग्राम (stone symbol of विष्णु); method of observing the दीपावली festival; on some more places of पिल्ग्रिमगे; greatness of the Bhagavadgītā explained through stories; importance of the Bhāgavata; description of certain hells, numbered here as 140; how a bath in a sacred river in the month of Māgha (11th lunar month, generally in February) purifies even a great sinner; certain ritu-alistic processes connected with the मन्त्र of Lord विष्णु; the story of churning the ocean of milk to get अमृत or ambrosia; the ten avatāras or incarnations of विष्णु.
On the whole, it can be stated that this purāṇa, which might have evolved over the period A. D. 600 to 1400, though it extols the greatness of विष्णु, is not antagonistic to शिव (who is also greatly revered here). It also gives a lot of information about the places of पिल्ग्रिमगे in India.

Padmāvatī
------------------------------------------
Padmāvatī is one of the names of लक्ष्मी, the divine consort of विष्णु/ नारायण. Since she emerged from the क्षीरसमुद्र (See SAMUDRAMATHANA.) with padmas or lotus flowers in her hands, she was called ‘Padmāvatī’.
According to the local legends of Tirumala/Tirupati—the famous place of Vaiṣṇava pilgrimage—Padmāvatī was the daughter of one king Ākāśarāja and was married to Veṅkaṭeśvara (the central deity of Tirumala). Even today this marriage—known as ‘Padmāvatīpariṇaya’ (or ‘kalyā-ṇotsava’)—is often ceremonially celebrated by the temple authorities as per the desire of the devotees.
At Tirucānūr, 3 kms. (2 miles) from the तिरुपति railway station, there is a big temple of पद्मावती who is known (in Tamil) as ‘Alarmelmaṅgai’.

padma
(‘lotus’)
------------------------------------------
‘Padma’ is one of the most widely used words in the सन्स्क्रित् लन्गुअगे with a variety of meanings such as: lotus flower, certain marks on the face of an elephant, a particular formation of an army, the चक्रस् (psychic centres in the body), one of the nine treasures of कुबेर (the god of wealth) and the number 1019.
However, the lotus also is widely used as a symbol and a decorative motif in temples and other types of buildings. Its symbolical significance may be explained as follows:
The lotus bud is born in water and unfolds itself into a beautiful flower. Hence it is taken as a symbol of the universe coming out of the primeval waters and manifesting itself in all its glory. It is also taken as a symbol of the sun. It rises from the navel of विष्णु and is the seat of ब्रह्मा, the creator. Hence the sacredness associated with it.
The Mahābhārata (Sabhāparva 9; Śāntiparva 363-371) mentions one पद्म, as a king of serpents, extremely sagacious and full of great wisdom.
Padmā is one of the names of the goddess लक्ष्मी, since she is seated on a lotus and wears a lotus garland.

padmāsana
(‘the lotus-posture’)
------------------------------------------
The पद्मासन is a posture recommended in the works on हठयोग for meditation. In this posture, one has to sit with both the legs crossed, to resemble a full-bloomed lotus (padma = lotus). It is said to destroy all diseases.
Many images in temples, in the āsīna or sitting postures, are in the पद्मासन pose.
See also ĀSANA.

Padmapāda
(9th century A. D.)
------------------------------------------
Born in a place in South India (Tamil Nadu) on the bank of the river कावेरी, पद्मपाद went to काशी (Vārāṇasī, modern Banaras in the State of Uttar Pradesh) for his एदुचतिओन्. There he met शङ्कर (A. D. 788-820) and became his disciple. He is said to have been शङ्कर’s first apostle.
It is said that he was once washing the clothes of his गुरु शङ्कर, standing on the bank of a river. शङ्कर, who was sitting on the opposite side of the river called him urgently for some work. Then Padmapāda—whose earlier name is not known—set out immediately walking on the water! A पद्म or a lotus started appearing below his pāda or foot supporting him! Hence the name ‘Padmapāda’.
His commentary on the Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya of शङ्कर was the earliest of such commentaries. It was supposed to be in two parts, the first being known as Pañcapādikā and the later part as Vṛtti.
The story goes that the manuscript of the entire commentary written by him was destroyed by his uncle smitten by jealousy. However, a part of it was retrieved by him since his गुरु शङ्कर, who had heard it read out to him—and, शङ्कर was endowed with a photographic memory—dictated that portion, viz., the first five pādas or quarters (out of the total of sixteen). The name of the commentary, Pañcapādikā, is based on this fact.
However, the commentary on the first four sūtras only is available now.
Prakāśātman (A. D. 1200) has written a gloss on this, known as Pañcapādikā-vivaraṇa, further amplifying पद्मपाद’s views. This has developed into a separate and special school of Advaita Vedānta called the Vivaraṇaprasthāna.
Padmapāda was a worshipper of the नरसिṁह aspect of Lord विष्णु and had once saved the life of his गुरु from the hands of the Kāpālikas.
See also ADVAITA VEDĀNTA DARŚANA.

Padmanābha Temple
------------------------------------------
Temples and places of worship, especially those connected with the lives of great saints or miraculous incidents, have been an integral part of Hindu religion and culture. Places associated with such temples, soon become important centres of पिल्ग्रिमगे, attracting thousands of devotees every year especially on special occasions.
One such place in the extremity of South India is the पद्मनाभ तेम्प्ले of Tiruvanantapuram (or Trivandrum), the Capital of the Kerala State. It is a विष्णु temple with the image in the śayāna or reclining posture, resting on the great serpent अनन्त (or शेष). Hence, it is also known as the Anantaśayana Temple. Since the image of विष्णु has पद्म or lotus with ब्रह्मा (the creator) seated on it, he is also known as Padmanābha or Padmanābhasvāmi (one who has the lotus in his navel).
Considered one among the 108 विष्णु temples sacred to the followers of the विष्णु cult, it has been praised by नम्माऌवार्, the last of the आऌवार्स् (in his Tiruvāymoḷi). (See ĀḶVĀRS.) Since he is assigned to the 9th century A. D., this temple must be considered as much older than that period.
Padmanābha Temple at TiruvanantapuramThere are several local legends that describe how this temple came into being. The Lord is said to have revealed Himself in this form to the sage Divākaramuni who was an ardent devotee of कृष्ण.
According to another version, the revelation came to the sage Vilvamaṅgal (known as Vilvamaṅgalattu Svāmiyār in Malayāḷam language) who saw the Lord in a place in a forest, where a big tree collapsed, giving rise to the vision.
It is reasonable to believe that though the temple is quite ancient, it must have undergone several renovations and changes.
The temple seems to have been connected with several royal dynasties like the Ay dynasty (300 B. C.), the Cera kings (of Tamil Nadu and Kerala) and the rulers of Venad (in Kerala).
The most significant event in the history of this temple is the total surrender of the kingdom to the Lord Padmanābha by the famous king Mārtāṇḍa Varma (during his rule in A. D. 1729-1758), who assumed the title ‘Padmanābhadāsa’ and started ruling as the Lord’s servant. He is said to have reconstructed the temple including the replacement of the old idol made of wood, with a new one fashioned out of 1200 Śālagrāmas (round stone-emblems of विष्णु).
The temple faces east and is spread out over an area of 2.8 hectares (7 acres). It is enclosed on all sides by a high granite wall, the height ranging from 4.5 to 6.0 metres (15 to 20 ft.).
The गर्भगृह (sanctum sanctorum) is a rectangle measuring 7.2 metres (24 ft.) in length, 5.4 metres (18 ft.) in width and 12 metres (40 ft.) in height.
The reclining image of Lord पद्म-nābha is 5.4 metres (18 ft.) in length. It is facing east, with the head to the south and the feet to the north. From the नाभि or navel, rises a पद्म or lotus on which is a small figure of ब्रह्मा, the four faced creator of the world. The serpent अनन्त (or शेष) has five hoods and three coils, the latter forming the bed for the Lord and the former acting as a protective umbrella.
The posture is Yogaśayana and the idol itself is classed among the Uttama-योग-mūrtis.
Since the outer part of the image is made of wood of certain medicinal trees and a mixture called katusarkarayoga, ceremonial bathing with water is never performed.
There are three main doors for the sanctum, to see the image, the three giving a view of the head or the face, the navel and the feet.
Other important structures and features of this temple-complex are: ध्वज-stambha (wooden flagstaff covered with gold plates and 24 metres or 80 ft. in height); temples or shrines of other deities like Rāmasvāmi, Narasiṁhasvāmi, विष्वक्सेन, गणपति, शिव, and शास्ता (Ayyappa); Śrībalipura (a long paved corridor running all round, with 324 pillars and a covered roof); the Oṭṭakkal-maṇṭapa, a pavilion made of one huge stone; the Kulaśekhara maṇṭapa containing several beautifully sculptured images; mural paintings inside the sanctum and many other features.
When one presses his ear against the northern outer wall of the sanctum, he hears the ‘sounds of waves,’ believed to be those of the क्षीरसमुद्र (the ocean of milk) on which the Lord is resting!
The temple has four chief priests called ‘nambies’. They are assisted by 24 pottis or assistant priests.
Daily rituals start at 3:30 A.M. and come to a close by late night. There are also quite a few monthly, bi-annual and annual rites.
The most important and spectacular festival is the Murajapam, followed by the Lakṣadīpam. It is celebrated once in six years and is spread over 56 days. During the latter festival, the entire gopuram (tower) and other parts of the temple are lighted with oil lamps giving a magnificent view of the gopuram in the waters of the temple-tank.
This festival, as is conducted now, is said to be only a faint shadow of the original grand festival, the last of which was held in A. D. 1960.
See also ANANTAŚAYANA.

padmapīṭha
(‘seat of [an icon shaped like a] lotus’)
------------------------------------------
Building of हिन्दु तेम्प्लेस् and installing of images in them is done strictly in accordance with a well-developed science—of architecture and इचोनोग्रफ्य्.
Every mūrti or image ceremonially installed in a temple for worship, must have a पीठ (seat or pedestal) whose size is decided by the size of the image or that of the door of the sanctum. There are several varieties of them of which the पद्मपीठ is also one.
This पीठ or pedestal is of the shape of a पद्म or a lotus. There may be one or two; in the latter case they are abutted against each other, the lower one being inverted.

pādakṛcchra
(‘kṛcchra of four aspects’)
------------------------------------------
Man is often prone to committing sins due to the weaknesses of the flesh. However, religions generally provide him with ways and means of redeeming himself.
Hinduism prescribes two steps for such redemption: paścāttāpa (repentance) and प्रायश्चित्त (expiation).
The most general name for prāyaścittas is ‘kṛcchra’. Out of the several varieties of कृच्छ्र, the पादकृच्छ्र is also one. In this expiation, the transgressor of धर्म has to take ड़ोओद् only once by day (on the first day of expiation), once only by night on the second day, once at any time (if he gets the ड़ोओद् unasked) on the third day and observe a total fast on the fourth day.
Even the quantity of ड़ोओद् allowed on the first three days is restricted by the धर्मशास्त्रस्.
See also KṚCCHRA.
